question: Why do surgeons place a surgical drain?

options.B: To prevent fluid from building up and causing infection
options.C: To stop the need for antibiotics
options.D: To help the body reabsorb blood

explanation: Drains stop blood, serum, or pus from pooling, which lowers the chance of bacteria growing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h1)

question: When is a prophylactic drain used?

options.A: After an infection has already started
options.B: Before surgery to empty the bowel
options.C: To treat a confirmed internal abscess
options.D: During surgery to stop expected fluid buildup

explanation: Prophylactic drains are placed when a surgeon expects extra fluid or blood after an operation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h1)

question: Which of these is an example of an open drainage system?
explanation: A Penrose drain is an open system that lets fluid drain straight onto dressings outside the body. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h2)

question: Why are closed drainage systems preferred over open systems?

options.A: They lower the risk of germs traveling back into the body
options.B: They let fluid evaporate through the plastic
options.C: They mean nurses never need to check them
options.D: They do not rely on gravity

explanation: Sealed tubing stops environmental germs from easily moving backward into body tissues. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h2)

question: What is the main job of a nasogastric tube attached to suction?

options.A: Emptying fluid and gas from the stomach

explanation: Suction through an NG tube clears out stomach contents to stop bloating, nausea, and vomiting. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h3)

question: Why must a urine bag always hang lower than the patient's bladder?

options.A: To stop urine from flowing backward into the bladder
options.B: To keep pressure high in the tube
options.C: To help the kidneys make urine faster
options.D: To make it easier for the nurse to read without bending

explanation: Gravity keeps urine moving away from the body. Raising the bag causes urine to flow backward, which can lead to an infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h3)

question: What does a sudden stop in fluid from a surgical drain usually mean?

options.C: The tube is blocked or kinked
options.D: The body has stopped making fluid

explanation: A sudden drop in output is usually caused by a physical blockage in the tube rather than an overnight cure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h4)

question: What should you do right away if bright red blood suddenly fills a surgical drain?

options.A: Clamp the drain so no more blood leaves
options.B: Lower the collection bag to the floor
options.C: Call the surgical team about possible bleeding
options.D: Flush the tube with sterile normal saline

explanation: Bright red bleeding points to active bleeding inside that needs quick medical attention. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h4)

question: Why do you need to squeeze bulb-style suction drains before putting the cap back on?

options.A: To create the suction needed to pull out fluid
options.B: To clean the inside of the chamber
options.C: To keep the plastic from cracking
options.D: To push trapped air out through the drain site

explanation: Compressing the bulb and sealing it creates a vacuum that gently pulls fluid from the surgical site. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h5)

question: Why is it important to pin or secure drainage tubing to the patient's clothing?

options.B: To keep the collection bag hidden
options.C: To stop the drain from being accidentally pulled out
options.D: To warm up the fluid inside

explanation: Securing the tube gives it some slack so moving around doesn't yank the drain out of the wound. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h5)

question: Which action is dangerous if a surgical drain is accidentally pulled out partway?

options.A: Pushing the tubing back into the wound
options.C: Putting a sterile dressing over the opening

explanation: Pushing a slipped tube back inside carries skin germs straight into the sterile wound. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h6)

question: A patient's suction drain stops working, and the area becomes tight and painful. What should you check first?

options.A: Turn the suction pressure all the way up
options.C: Check the tubing for kinks or blood clots
options.D: Wash out the wound with tap water

explanation: Kinks and clots are the most common reasons a drain suddenly stops working. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h6)

question: Why is a patient asked to hold their breath or bear down when a drain is being removed?

options.A: To stop air from entering the empty tract

explanation: This breathing technique changes pressure in the body, lowering the risk of air getting into the tissue space. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h7)

question: What kind of dressing is usually put on right after a drain is taken out?

options.A: A sterile dressing that seals the wound
options.C: Wet gauze soaked in sterile water

explanation: An airtight dressing covers the opening to stop fluid leaks and keep bacteria out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h7)
